topic.title: Genetic engineering: producing human insulin
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: A Higher-paper question of seven to ten marks, set late in B2 Higher in 2019, 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025. The marks that separate candidates are the names (genome, restriction, sticky ends, downstreaming), the difference between the gene and the hormone, and, when it is set, the base-sequence part: marking staggered cuts and counting the sections.
mustMemorise: The genome is all the genetic material of an organism; genetic engineering changes it to give a desirable characteristic
A restriction enzyme cuts at one base sequence, with a staggered cut that leaves sticky ends
The same enzyme cuts the plasmid, so the sticky ends are complementary and the gene can join it
The joined ring is a modified plasmid (also called recombinant); the bacterium that takes it in is genetically modified
In the fermenter the bacteria multiply, their plasmids are copied, and they make proteins including human insulin, a protein built from amino acids
Downstreaming is extraction, purification and packaging, to give a pure form of insulin
Straight length: sections = cuts + 1. Ring: pieces = cuts
A labelled drawing needs the cell, the plasmid as two rings, the insulin gene marked, and one sticky end
notOnThisSpec: Ligase, the enzyme that joins the ends: CCEA names only the restriction enzyme
Viruses as vectors: CCEA's only vector is the bacterial plasmid
How a gene is read to build a protein (transcription and translation)
Genetically modified crops, herbicide and insect resistance
Gene therapy, cloning and the Human Genome Project
The names of particular restriction enzymes

note.title: Genetic engineering: producing human insulin
note.subject: science

mustKnow: Sections from a straight length of DNA = cuts + 1; pieces from a ring = cuts
The route: cut the gene out and the plasmid open with the same enzyme, join, put into a bacterium, multiply in a fermenter, downstream

notOnThisSpec: Ligase, the enzyme that joins the ends: CCEA names only the restriction enzyme
Viruses as vectors: CCEA's only vector is the bacterial plasmid
How a gene is read to build a protein (transcription and translation)
Genetically modified crops, herbicide and insect resistance
Gene therapy, cloning and the Human Genome Project
The names of particular restriction enzymes

mustBeAbleTo: Say what the genome is, and what genetic engineering changes and why
Describe the stages of making human insulin in order, naming the restriction enzyme, sticky ends, plasmid, fermenter and downstreaming
Find a restriction enzyme's sites in a base sequence, mark each staggered cut, and count the sections it leaves: cuts + 1, because a straight length already has two ends
Carry that method to any enzyme a stem describes, whatever its sequence and wherever it cuts
Explain why the same restriction enzyme cuts the gene and the plasmid
Say what the plasmid carries into the bacterium, and give four processes in the fermenter: the bacteria multiply, their plasmids are copied, they make proteins, they make insulin
Say that insulin is a protein made from amino acids, and why bacteria carrying the human gene make it
Name the three stages of downstreaming and say why it is needed
Draw and label the modified bacterium: the cell, the plasmid as two rings, the human insulin gene marked, one sticky end
Give the advantages of making human insulin this way
Finish the DNA chain the paper builds round this topic: a base percentage, the amino acids a length codes for, then the cuts
sheet.howExamined: Higher paper only. B2 Higher is 1 hour 15 minutes for 80 marks, calculator allowed. Every bullet of outcome 2.4.12 is Higher Tier, and CCEA has set this material late in the paper: Q9 in Summer 2019, Q10 in 2022, Q7 in 2023, Q10 in 2024 and part of Q10 in 2025, usually worth seven to ten marks (four in 2025, where it closed a question on DNA structure). The shapes: one-mark names and definitions every year (genome, restriction, sticky ends, downstreaming); a base sequence on which to mark the staggered cuts and count the sections (2019, 2025), in both years the last part of a question that began with base percentages and the number of amino acids a length codes for; a stage diagram with one stage to describe (2019, 2022); the fermenter's processes, asked as four, two and one (2022, 2023, 2024); a four-mark labelled drawing of the modified bacterium (2023); the hormone, protein, amino acids chain (2024).
traps: Marking the staggered cuts on a base sequence and counting the sections: on Summer 2025 B2 Higher Q10 only the more able candidates showed all three cuts staggered, and only the more able gave four sections for three cuts
Naming the ends: on Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q10 many candidates gave restriction for the enzyme, but fewer could name the sticky ends
Writing that the plasmid contains the hormone when the mark needs the gene (Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q10)
Saying what happens to the bacterium and its plasmid in the fermenter with anything but reproduce or multiply: Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q10 accepted only those

Answering a fermenter question with conditions (warm, fed, stirred) when it asks for processes: Summer 2022 B2 Higher Q10 wanted four processes, and its scheme credited the bacteria multiplying, the plasmids being copied, bacterial protein being made and insulin being made
Linking hormone, protein and amino acids: Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q10 found only the best candidates could say insulin is a protein made from amino acids
Naming the enzyme: Summer 2023 B2 Higher Q7 saw restriction given by many candidates, with many other enzyme names beside it

Drawing the modified bacterium: the Summer 2023 report says the drawings for B2 Higher Q7(b) were well below the standard expected, so draw both rings of DNA and label the plasmid, the human insulin gene and a sticky end

Defining the genome as a gene: it is all the genetic material of an organism. Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q10 rewarded the learned definition, and in Summer 2023 only the better candidates gave the word genome for B2 Higher Q7(a)
Calling the plasmid recombinant only: CCEA's papers and schemes call it the modified plasmid, so use that word and treat recombinant as its other name

This restriction enzyme cuts between T and C wherever the top strand reads TCGA from left to right. The bottom strand under each site reads TCGA from right to left, and it is cut between its own T and C.

steps.working: Read the top strand from the left and mark every TCGA: bases 3 to 6, 9 to 12, 14 to 17 and 20 to 23.
steps.decision: Find the sites before thinking about cuts. Every site is found on the top strand read left to right, so one sweep finds them all.

options: Because the bottom strand under each TCGA also reads TCGA, from right to left
Because the enzyme only ever cuts the top strand
Because the bottom strand has no sites of its own
whyMenu.explain: TCGA is its own partner read backwards, so wherever the top strand has a site the bottom strand has one too, directly underneath. One sweep of the top strand finds every site.

steps.working: Each site is one staggered cut through both strands: 4 cuts.
steps.decision: The top-strand cut and the bottom-strand cut at one site are two halves of the same staggered cut. Count sites, not strand cuts.

steps.working: A straight length already has two ends, so sections = cuts + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5.
steps.decision: Summer 2025 found only the more able candidates earned this mark. Adding one is the whole step.

steps.working: Ask what the molecule looks like before the enzyme arrives: a ring, with no free ends.
steps.decision: The shape decides the rule, so settle the shape first. A ring and a straight length count differently.

options: Because a ring has no ends and a straight length has two
Because a ring is shorter than a straight length
Because a ring is harder to cut
whyMenu.explain: It is the ends that matter. A straight length starts with two, so every cut adds a piece; a ring starts with none, so its first cut only opens it.

steps.working: The first cut only opens the ring into one long piece. Each later cut adds one piece.
steps.decision: Picture cutting a rubber band once: you still hold one piece.
Check against the drawing: the 3 cut marks divide the ring into 3 arcs.

steps.working: A restriction enzyme cuts wherever it finds one particular base sequence.
steps.decision: The first mark is about the enzyme's behaviour. Start there and the second mark follows from it.

options: Because it recognises one base sequence
Because it cuts anything it touches
Because it cuts only human DNA
whyMenu.explain: A restriction enzyme cuts at one recognition sequence, so it leaves the same shape of end on whatever DNA it cuts.

steps.working: So it cuts the gene and the plasmid at the same base sequence.
steps.decision: This is the first mark: same enzyme, same sequence.

steps.working: The sticky ends on the plasmid are complementary to the sticky ends on the gene, so they pair up and the gene joins the plasmid.
steps.decision: Finish on the consequence. An explain question is answered by the effect, and the effect needs the name sticky ends.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The enzyme cuts at the same base sequence every time, so the sticky ends are complementary and the gene can join the plasmid.

twin.stem: Explain what would happen if a different restriction enzyme were used to cut the plasmid. [1]

accepted: the sticky ends would not be complementary, so the gene could not join the plasmid

any: the gene could not be joined

workedExamples.stem: Modified bacteria carrying the human insulin gene are put into a fermenter. Give two things that happen in the fermenter which lead to human insulin being made. [2]

figure.alt: A stirred fermenter full of rod-shaped genetically modified bacteria.

steps.working: Name what the bacteria do: they multiply, or reproduce.
steps.decision: The question names the bacteria, so the first process is what the bacteria themselves do. Grow is not the word: the mark is for more of them.

options: Because a fermenter is for making billions of bacteria from a few
Because bacteria in a fermenter get bigger
Because the fermenter cuts the bacteria open

hints: A straight molecule already has two ends before any cut is made.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the rule for a ring. A straight molecule has two free ends before the enzyme touches it, so the number of pieces is one more than the number of cuts.
Only the first cut makes two pieces out of one. After that, one of the two pieces was already counted, so each further cut adds one.

parts.stem: The straight piece of DNA in the diagram is cut in 6 places. Give the number of pieces produced.
parts.workedSolution: A straight molecule already has two ends, so every cut adds one more piece: 6 + 1 = 7 pieces.

hints: The first cut on a ring makes no second piece: it only opens the ring.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the rule for a straight molecule. A ring has no free ends, so the first cut only opens it, and the number of pieces equals the number of cuts.

parts.stem: The circular plasmid in the diagram is cut in 6 places. Give the number of pieces produced.
parts.workedSolution: A ring has no ends, so its first cut only opens it. Each cut after that adds one piece, so 6 cuts give 6 pieces.

hints: Say what each shape has before the enzyme arrives: how many ends?
parts.stem: Explain why the two answers are different.

accepted: a straight molecule already has two ends, so every cut adds one more piece, while a circle has no ends and its first cut only opens the ring
the straight piece has two ends to start with, so each cut adds a piece, but the plasmid has no ends, so the first cut just opens it

any: straight molecule already has two ends
straight piece already has two ends

scheme.for: the straight molecule already has two (free) ends, so each cut adds one more piece
the circular plasmid has no ends, so its first cut only opens it into one piece

parts.workedSolution: A straight molecule already has two ends, so every cut adds one more piece, while a circle has no ends and its first cut only opens the ring.

parts.stem:
Describe how human insulin is produced by genetic engineering, from the human gene to the insulin that is given to a patient.

This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; the ideas are ordered very clearly and follow on from one another; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; the ideas are ordered reasonably well and mostly follow on; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; the organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

scheme.examinerNote: Two losses run through the reports on this material: Summer 2024 found answers that put the hormone rather than the gene inside the plasmid, and Summer 2025 found only the stronger candidates could place the staggered cuts. parts.workedSolution: A restriction enzyme cuts the insulin gene out of human DNA. Its staggered cut leaves sticky ends on the gene. A plasmid is taken from a bacterium and cut open with the same restriction enzyme, so its sticky ends are complementary to the gene's. The gene is joined into the plasmid, making a recombinant plasmid, and the plasmid is put into a bacterium, which is now a genetically modified bacterium. The modified bacteria multiply in a fermenter, and each one uses the human gene to make insulin. Finally, downstreaming: the insulin is extracted, purified and packaged, so that a pure form reaches the patient.

hints: T pairs with A, so A is present in the same amount.
C and G share whatever is left, equally.

commonErrors.feedback: That is what the other two bases have between them. They pair with each other, so they share it equally: halve it.
That takes only one base away from 100. The base in the question has a partner present in the same amount, so take both away, then halve what is left.
That is the percentage of the given base's own partner. A pairs with T and C pairs with G: the base you were asked for belongs to the other pair.
That halves the given percentage. Halve what is left after both bases of the given pair are taken from 100.

parts.stem:
In one length of DNA, 20% of the bases are T.
Calculate the percentage of the bases that are C. Show your working out.

scheme.for: A is 20% as well: 20 + 20 = 40

parts.workedSolution: T pairs with A, so A is 20% too: 40% together. 100 − 40 = 60% is shared by C and G, so C is 60 ÷ 2 = 30%.

hints: Three bases code for one amino acid.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the number of bases. Three bases code for one amino acid, so divide by three.
That multiplies by three. Each amino acid takes three bases, so the number of amino acids is the number of bases divided by three.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows a different length of DNA. One strand of it carries 24 bases.
How many amino acids does this length of DNA code for?
parts.workedSolution: Three bases code for one amino acid, so 24 bases code for 24 ÷ 3 = 8 amino acids.

hints: Find each TCGA on the top strand, reading from the left.
The cut goes between the T and the C of each site, so its gap number is the number of the T.

commonErrors.feedback: Those are the gaps where the bottom strand is cut. On the top strand each cut comes two bases earlier, between the T and the C read from the left.

parts.stem:
This restriction enzyme cuts between T and C wherever the top strand reads TCGA from left to right. The bottom strand under each site reads TCGA from right to left, and it is cut between its own T and C.
The gaps between the bases are numbered. Give the number of every gap in which the top strand is cut.

accepted: gaps 3, 9 and 18

scheme.for: gap 3 (the top strand of the site at bases 3 to 6)
gap 9 (the top strand of the site at bases 9 to 12)
gap 18 (the top strand of the site at bases 18 to 21)

parts.workedSolution: TCGA appears at bases 3 to 6, 9 to 12 and 18 to 21 of the top strand. The cut is between T and C, so the top strand is cut in gaps 3, 9 and 18.

hints: Count the staggered cuts, then remember what a straight length has before it is cut.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the number of cuts. A straight length already has two ends, so the number of sections is one more than the number of cuts. Summer 2025 found only the more able candidates gave the right number of sections.
That counts each strand's cut separately. The two halves of a staggered cut make one cut through the whole molecule, so count the sites, then add one.

parts.stem: Give the number of sections this length of DNA is cut into.
parts.workedSolution: 3 staggered cuts on a straight length of DNA give 3 + 1 = 4 sections.

hints: Start with what a restriction enzyme does every time it cuts.
Then say what that means for the two sets of sticky ends.
parts.stem: The section between the first and second cuts is the gene wanted. It is joined into a plasmid that has been cut open with the same restriction enzyme. Explain why the same enzyme must be used.

accepted: it cuts at the same base sequence every time, so the sticky ends on the plasmid are complementary to the sticky ends on the gene and the two can join
it recognises the same base sequence in both, so the ends match and the gene can be joined into the plasmid

any: cuts at the same base sequence

scheme.for: the enzyme cuts at the same base sequence every time (accept: in the same place)
so the sticky ends are complementary / match, and the gene can join the plasmid

parts.workedSolution: It cuts at the same base sequence every time, so the sticky ends on the plasmid are complementary to the sticky ends on the gene and the two can join.

hints: Two names, one mark each.

commonErrors.feedback: The enzyme that cuts DNA at a particular base sequence is a restriction enzyme. Summer 2023 found many other enzyme names offered for this mark.

parts.stem: The diagram shows a length of human DNA that has been cut and pulled apart. Name the type of enzyme that made this cut, and name the ends marked (i) and (ii).

accepted: a restriction enzyme, which leaves sticky ends

scheme.for: restriction (enzyme)
sticky ends

parts.workedSolution: A restriction enzyme, which leaves sticky ends.

hints: The ends were cut by the same enzyme, so they fit.
The plasmid's name says that it has been changed.
parts.stem: The same enzyme is used to cut open a plasmid. Describe how the insulin gene becomes part of the plasmid, and give the name used for the plasmid that results.

accepted: the complementary sticky ends of the gene and the plasmid pair up and are joined, making a modified plasmid

any: sticky ends of the gene and the plasmid pair

scheme.for: the complementary sticky ends pair up / join (so the gene is joined into the gap)
modified plasmid (accept: recombinant plasmid)

parts.workedSolution: The complementary sticky ends of the gene and the plasmid pair up and are joined, making a modified plasmid, also called a recombinant plasmid.

hints: Say what has been added, then say what that does to the bacterium's genetic material.
parts.stem: The plasmid is then put into a bacterium. Explain why the bacterium is described as genetically modified.

accepted: it now carries a gene it did not have before, the human insulin gene, so its genetic material has been changed

any: a new gene has been added

scheme.for: it now has a gene it did not have before (the human insulin gene)
so its genome / genetic material has been changed

parts.workedSolution: It now carries a gene it did not have before, the human insulin gene, so its genetic material has been changed.

hints: C pairs with G, so G is present in the same amount.
A and T share whatever is left, equally.

commonErrors.feedback: That is what the other two bases have between them. They pair with each other, so they share it equally: halve it.
That takes only one base away from 100. The base in the question has a partner present in the same amount, so take both away, then halve what is left.
That is the percentage of the given base's own partner. A pairs with T and C pairs with G: the base you were asked for belongs to the other pair.
That halves the given percentage. Halve what is left after both bases of the given pair are taken from 100.

parts.stem:
In a length of DNA, 22% of the bases are C.
Calculate the percentage of the bases that are A. Show your working out.

scheme.for: G is 22% as well: 22 + 22 = 44

parts.workedSolution: C pairs with G, so G is 22% too: 44% together. 100 − 44 = 56% is shared by A and T, so A is 56 ÷ 2 = 28%.

hints: A ring has no ends before it is cut.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the rule for a straight length. A ring has no free ends, so the first cut only opens it, and the number of pieces equals the number of cuts.

parts.stem: A restriction enzyme finds its site 4 times around a circular plasmid. Give the number of pieces the plasmid is cut into.
parts.workedSolution: A ring has no ends, so its first cut only opens it: 4 cuts give 4 pieces.

hints: A straight length already has two ends before the enzyme touches it.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the rule for a ring. A straight length has two free ends before the enzyme touches it, so the number of sections is one more than the number of cuts.

parts.stem: The same enzyme finds its site 4 times along a straight length of DNA. Give the number of sections produced.
parts.workedSolution: A straight length already has two ends, so every cut adds a section: 4 + 1 = 5 sections.

findTheMistake.stem: Ciara is given a length of DNA and told that a restriction enzyme cuts it wherever the top strand reads TCGA. She is asked how many sections it will be cut into. Her working:
studentWorking: TCGA appears 3 times on the top strand.
Each site is one staggered cut, so there are 3 cuts.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are right. Line 3 gives the number of cuts as the number of sections. A straight length of DNA already has two ends, so every cut adds one more section: 3 cuts make 4 sections.
correction: TCGA appears 3 times on the top strand.
Each site is one staggered cut, so there are 3 cuts.
findTheMistake.feedback: The sites and the cuts were found correctly, and that is the harder half. Summer 2025 records that only the more able candidates gave the right number of sections here: counting cuts and forgetting the extra piece is exactly how the mark goes.

findTheMistake.stem: Conor is asked to describe three stages of making human insulin, one mark each. His answer:
studentWorking: The insulin gene is joined into a plasmid cut with the same restriction enzyme.
The plasmid carries insulin into the bacterium.
The bacteria multiply in a fermenter.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 3 are correct and well worded. Line 2 puts the hormone inside the plasmid. What the plasmid carries is the human insulin gene. No insulin exists until the bacterium makes it from that gene.
correction: The insulin gene is joined into a plasmid cut with the same restriction enzyme.
The plasmid carries the human insulin gene into the bacterium.
The bacteria multiply in a fermenter.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two of the three marks stand. The report for Summer 2024 names this one: candidates wrote that the plasmid contained the hormone when the mark needed the gene. One word, gene, is the whole difference.

findTheMistake.stem: Aoife is asked what happens in the fermenter and what happens next, one mark each. Her answer:
studentWorking: The genetically modified bacteria are placed in a fermenter.
In the fermenter, the bacteria and their plasmids grow.
Afterwards the insulin is extracted, purified and packaged.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 3 are right. Line 2 says the bacteria and plasmids grow, but the mark is for making more of them: they multiply, or reproduce. A few bacteria growing bigger would make very little insulin.
correction: The genetically modified bacteria are placed in a fermenter.
In the fermenter, the bacteria and their plasmids multiply.
Afterwards the insulin is extracted, purified and packaged.
findTheMistake.feedback: Two marks stand. Summer 2024 accepted only reproduction or multiplication for this part, because the question was about the bacterium and its plasmid together. Grow is the word that cost the mark.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh is given a length of DNA whose top strand reads GTTCGACATCCTCGAAGTCGAC, and told that the enzyme cuts between T and C wherever it finds TCGA, reading either way. She is asked for the gap numbers in which the top strand and the bottom strand are cut at the first site, one mark each. Her working:
studentWorking: TCGA is at bases 3 to 6 of the top strand.
The top strand is cut between T and C: gap 3.
The bottom strand is cut straight across, in gap 3 as well.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are right. Line 3 cuts straight across. The bottom strand under the site reads TCGA from right to left, so its cut between T and C falls two bases further along, in gap 5. The two cuts are staggered, which is what leaves the sticky ends.
correction: TCGA is at bases 3 to 6 of the top strand.
The top strand is cut between T and C: gap 3.
The bottom strand is cut between its own T and C, read right to left: two bases along, in gap 5.
findTheMistake.feedback: The site and the top-strand cut are right, and that is the first mark. Summer 2025 found only the more able candidates drew the cuts staggered: a cut straight across both strands leaves no sticky ends, and it loses the second mark.

prompts.answer: Changing the genome of an organism to give it a desirable characteristic.

prompts.prompt: Name the type of enzyme that cuts the insulin gene out of human DNA, and name the ends it leaves.
prompts.answer: A restriction enzyme, and it leaves sticky ends.

prompts.prompt: Why is the same restriction enzyme used on the human DNA and on the plasmid?
prompts.answer: It cuts at the same base sequence both times, so the sticky ends are complementary and the gene can join the plasmid.

prompts.prompt: A restriction enzyme finds its site n times along a straight length of DNA. How many sections are made? And on a ring?
prompts.answer: A straight length gives n + 1 sections, because it already has two ends. A ring gives n pieces, because the first cut only opens it.

prompts.prompt: What makes a restriction enzyme's cut staggered?
prompts.answer: It cuts the two strands at different points, a few bases apart, which leaves single-stranded sticky ends.
A plasmid that has had a gene from another organism joined into it: here, the human insulin gene.

prompts.prompt: Does the plasmid carry insulin or the insulin gene into the bacterium?
prompts.answer: The insulin gene. The bacterium makes the insulin from it afterwards.

prompts.prompt: What happens to the modified bacteria and their plasmids in the fermenter?
prompts.answer: They multiply: the bacteria reproduce, the plasmids are copied, and each bacterium makes human insulin.

prompts.prompt: What are the three stages of downstreaming, and why is it needed?
prompts.answer: Extraction, purification and packaging. It is needed so that a pure form of insulin reaches the patient.

prompts.prompt: Give three advantages of making human insulin with genetically modified bacteria.
prompts.answer: It is identical to human insulin, it can be made in large quantities and cheaply, and no animal is used.

prompts.prompt: What four things does a labelled drawing of the modified bacterium need?
prompts.answer: The cell, the plasmid drawn as two rings, the human insulin gene marked and labelled on the plasmid, and one sticky end labelled.

prompts.prompt: Name four processes in the fermenter that lead to human insulin being made.
prompts.answer: The bacteria multiply, their plasmids are copied, the bacteria make their own proteins, and they make human insulin.

prompts.prompt: In the base-sequence question, where exactly is each strand cut?
prompts.answer: The top strand between the two bases the stem names, reading left to right; the bottom strand between the same two bases reading right to left, so a few bases further along: a staggered cut.

prompts.prompt: A restriction enzyme cuts a length of DNA in n places. How many sections if the DNA is straight, and how many if it is a ring?
prompts.answer: Straight: n + 1 sections. Ring: n pieces, because the first cut only opens it.

prompts.prompt: In the base-sequence question, where is each strand cut?
prompts.answer: Top strand between the named bases, reading left to right; bottom strand the same, reading right to left: a staggered cut.

checks.tool: claude (author-unit-batch pass, B2 §2.4 batch D; every number generated in scratchpad/b2-batch-d)
checks.detail: Recomputed from scratchpad/b2-batch-d/data.mjs and seq.mjs: the sites of TCGA in every printed sequence are found by code (practice GATCGAACCTCGATTC: 2 sites, 3 sections; exam GTTCGACATCCTCGAAGTCGAC: 3 sites, top-strand gaps 3, 12, 18, bottom-strand gaps 5, 14, 20, 4 sections; the chain GCTCGAACTCGAGGTACTCGATGC: 3 sites, top-strand gaps 3, 9, 18, bottom-strand gaps 5, 11, 20, 4 sections, 24 bases coding for 8 amino acids); the second enzyme GGATCC, cut after its first base, in ACTGGATCCTTAGCGGATCCATGCTA: 2 sites, top-strand gaps 4, 15, bottom-strand gaps 8, 19, 3 sections, 4-base sticky ends; base pairing (20% T gives 30% C; 22% C gives 28% A); the fragment rule (a straight molecule cut in 6 places gives 7 pieces, a ring 6; 4 sites give 4 pieces on a ring and 5 sections on a line); and downstreaming that recovers 190 g of 250 g is 76%. Every numeric distractor is an executed error route (routes.mjs): cuts counted as sections, each strand's cut counted separately, the bottom strand cut straight across or two bases along for the six-base site, the ring and line rules swapped, two pieces per cut, the sticky end given as the whole site or as the first enzyme's, the base pair's total not halved or only one copy subtracted or the partner's own value given or the given value halved, the bases not divided by three or multiplied by it, the percentage inverted, and the percentage lost given for the percentage recovered.

checks.tool: claude (author-unit-batch pass, B2 §2.4 batch D; every number generated in scratchpad/b2-batch-d)

Every citation carries the report's own question label, read by position in the report PDF; the 2023 findings sit beside the report's Q7 label (the private extraction had filed them in its Q8 and Q9 blocks, and the citations were corrected to Q7 on 23 Sep 2026). The shapes without a report on disk (Summer 2022 Q10's four processes, Summer 2019 Q9's stage diagram) are taken from the papers and their schemes, read in full.

checks.detail: Recomputed from scratchpad/b2-batch-d/data.mjs and seq.mjs: the sites of TCGA in every printed sequence are found by code (practice GATCGAACCTCGATTC: 2 sites, 3 sections; exam GTTCGACATCCTCGAAGTCGAC: 3 sites, top-strand gaps 3, 12, 18, bottom-strand gaps 5, 14, 20, 4 sections; the chain GCTCGAACTCGAGGTACTCGATGC: 3 sites, top-strand gaps 3, 9, 18, bottom-strand gaps 5, 11, 20, 4 sections, 24 bases coding for 8 amino acids); the second enzyme GGATCC, cut after its first base, in ACTGGATCCTTAGCGGATCCATGCTA: 2 sites, top-strand gaps 4, 15, bottom-strand gaps 8, 19, 3 sections, 4-base sticky ends; base pairing (20% T gives 30% C; 22% C gives 28% A); the fragment rule (a straight molecule cut in 6 places gives 7 pieces, a ring 6; 4 sites give 4 pieces on a ring and 5 sections on a line); and downstreaming that recovers 190 g of 250 g is 76%. Every numeric distractor is an executed error route (routes.mjs): cuts counted as sections, each strand's cut counted separately, the bottom strand cut straight across or two bases along for the six-base site, the ring and line rules swapped, two pieces per cut, the sticky end given as the whole site or as the first enzyme's, the base pair's total not halved or only one copy subtracted or the partner's own value given or the given value halved, the bases not divided by three or multiplied by it, the percentage inverted, and the percentage lost given for the percentage recovered.
